title: Equivalent names yield inconsistent factual answers in two language models
short_title: Different answers for names of the same object
abstract: When two names refer to the same object, asking about either name should give the same factual answer. If 'cat' and 'basket' name the same imaginary object, its home should not depend on which name appears in the question. We tested this requirement in two language models, Qwen3-4B and Phi-3.5-mini, using the same 32 fictional lists of objects, names, and properties. All facts needed to answer were written in the input. Qwen answered 1,657 of 2,304 factual questions correctly, and Phi answered 1,980. All 647 Qwen errors gave another listed object's value for the requested property; Phi made this kind of error 260 times. One name gave a correct answer while the other gave a wrong-object answer in 23 lists for Qwen and 14 for Phi. We then changed one small part of Qwen's calculation, copying its pattern of weights across the object descriptions from a calculation that answered correctly. An initial search looked promising, but the unchanged method corrected only one of eight complete wrong answers in six other development lists, while preserving ten correct answers. Further tests on those same six lists added no repairs. Some changes improved the score for the start of the correct answer relative to the original wrong one, without changing the answer produced. Thus, finding an internal pattern that affects an answer is not enough to show that it explains or reliably repairs the mistake. The cause of these errors remains unresolved. The internal tests used small, selected sets of cases and did not provide independent confirmation.

blocks.text: Introduction

Suppose a short list says that 'cat' and 'basket' are two names for the same imaginary object. Asking where cat lives and where basket lives should give the same answer. A language model must connect each name to that object and then return the requested fact. The facts are already in the input, so the task does not require outside knowledge. Yet a model can return a plausible fact about a different listed object. We ask when this happens and whether a change inside the model can correct it.

Earlier studies have found related problems. Yang showed that a model can follow familiar programming-library names instead of the explicit naming rules in the input, even when it correctly identifies the library [1]. Gur-Arieh and colleagues distinguished ways of finding an object through its name, its position in a list, or a more direct internal link [2]. Other work has studied how models track changes in which objects belong together and how they organize information about objects and their relationships [3,4]. These findings leave an important practical question: if an internal pattern appears to point to the right object, will copying that pattern make a wrong answer correct on other cases?

A proposed repair should produce the intended answer without damaging answers that were already correct. RAVEL, a benchmark for changing one fact while preserving others, makes this requirement explicit [5]. Likewise, an attention pattern shows how a model weights earlier text, but does not by itself explain the answer [6,7]. Tests that replace internal calculations, often called activation patching, depend on what is replaced, what it is compared with, and how success is measured [8]. A stronger explanation must show that the proposed internal change produces the predicted change in behavior, not just that the two are associated [9].

We tested two language models trained to follow instructions. Each input described four imaginary objects, their colors, shapes and homes, and additional names called aliases. Two aliases named the same object. We varied names, object labels, list positions, wording, and which name was highlighted, while keeping the correct answers unchanged within each comparison. We then changed one component in one model. We copied how it divided its attention across the four object descriptions during a correct calculation, rather than directly copying a complete correct answer.

Both models gave inconsistent answers for names of the same object. The proposed internal repair was less successful: an encouraging initial result weakened on other development examples, and further tests of the same component found no reliable fix even when prediction scores improved. The study documents this naming failure and tests one possible repair; it does not establish a new general explanation of how models link names to objects. We report separately the answer tests, the search for a component to change, the later test of that fixed change, and the follow-up analysis of the same failed cases. None is presented as final independent confirmation.
Materials and methods
Object lists and question design

We generated and evaluated 32 development lists, called worlds in the code. Each listed four imaginary objects with permanent labels A through D, a display nameplate, and different colors, shapes, and homes. We call the line describing one object its record, and each property a field. Four additional names were assigned to objects: two named the same target object, two named different objects, and one object had no additional name. For each property, the complete ordered assignment of values to objects differed between worlds, although individual words could recur. The model had to look up facts supplied in the input, not recall facts about real countries, people, or companies.

For each world, we exchanged the two names of the target object between their positions in the list of naming rules. This changed their order but not what they named or which answers were correct. We combined each name order with four highlighting choices: neither name, the first name, the second name, or an unrelated name. Each of these eight versions had nine property questions, two questions asking for an object's permanent label, and one asking for the list's status word. Each world therefore supplied 96 questions: 72 property questions, 16 label questions, and eight status questions. Each model received 3,072 questions in total, including 2,304 property questions.

We used two wording formats equally often. The target object's record position and the first equivalent name's position in the naming rules covered all 16 combinations equally often. The generator also balanced permanent object labels, which words filled the different naming roles, and the order of the two equivalent names. Other combinations were chosen randomly; the study did not test every possible combination of all factors. The additional names were apple, bat, anchor, date, cat, basket, fig, and dog. We selected these words using the two models' fixed text-processing rules before examining any answers. This tests whether models follow naming rules given in the input, not how well they distinguish all the meanings of words in ordinary language.

A world, rather than an individual question, was the independent unit of the dataset. Different names, highlights, properties, and repeated questions within a world share the same underlying facts. Both models received the same 32 worlds; using two models did not create 64 independent worlds. We also generated 64 reserved worlds and converted their text into model inputs, but did not run the models on them. Earlier project experiments with different tasks or smaller samples are not part of this study.
Models and answer generation

We used Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 and Phi-3.5-mini-instruct [10,11]. We fixed the exact model versions, text-processing files, prompts, and code, recording checksums so later copies could be checked against them. Model weights were not trained or updated during the study. Both models used 32-bit floating-point arithmetic, eager attention, one question at a time, and disabled TensorFloat-32 on an NVIDIA A40. The software versions were Python 3.12.15, PyTorch 2.6.0 with CUDA 12.4, and Transformers 5.14.1. S1 Appendix and the released records give the exact model revisions and remaining settings. These choices support repeatable numerical comparisons, not a claim about the fastest way to run the models.

Each prompt asked for only the requested property. The additional name appeared before an explicit boundary marker, followed by the requested property. Models process text in pieces called tokens. At each generation step we chose the highest-scoring next token, a rule called greedy generation. Generation stopped only at the configured end marker or after eight tokens. We removed only a final end marker when converting the answer to text; other special tokens remained. We counted an answer as correct only if its entire text matched the listed answer after ignoring case, whitespace differences, and final punctuation. We did not turn an explanation, a prefixed answer, or an unfinished response into a correct answer by keeping only its convenient part.
How answers were scored

A wrong-object answer was a finished response giving the requested property of another listed object. Because the objects had different values for each property, we could identify these answers without ambiguity. We counted other errors, including extra text and unfinished responses, separately. Within each world, name order, highlighting choice, and property, we compared questions using the two names of the same object. The main disagreement measure required one answer to be correct and the other to be a finished wrong-object answer. There were 24 such pairs per world and 768 per model. We also recorded broader measures, such as any difference in answer text or any pair with exactly one correct answer, but did not treat them as the same outcome.

Before studying internal calculations, we required each model to make wrong-object errors in at least 12 worlds and to have at least 24 of the main paired disagreements across at least eight worlds. This rule checked that there were enough examples to investigate; it was neither a statistical significance test nor evidence of novelty. Questions asking for permanent object labels used the same strict whole-answer rule. We later examined whether formatting explained some label errors, but did not use this more permissive check to replace the original score.
Testing an internal repair

We changed internal calculations only in Qwen. We selected worlds in which one name produced correct answers to all three property questions and the permanent-label question, while the other name of that object produced at least one finished wrong-object answer. The correct calculation supplied the pattern to copy, so we call it the source or donor. The calculation being changed is the recipient. A repeatable ordering based on checksums selected one context per qualifying world. Fourteen worlds qualified: eight were used to search for a useful change, and six were initially kept out of that search. All 14 had already been used in the answer tests. Reopening the same six worlds later was further exploration, not a second independent test.

The first search changed calculations at the marker after the name but before the requested property appeared. We replaced attention outputs across nonfinal processing layers, then tested individual attention heads in two selected layers. An attention head is a small component that assigns weights to earlier text positions and combines the information they supply, stored as value vectors, into an output. The early changes had weak effects and did not establish a repair of complete answers. We then examined the head calculations at the point where the model began answering. In each of the eight search cases, we saved unchanged calculations for both equivalent names, using the color question and a repeatably selected property question that the model answered incorrectly.

We located each object's record using its printed line and the mapping between text characters and tokens. This did not require knowing which object was the correct one. For each head, we measured its total attention weight on all four records, the share going to each record, and the relative token weights inside each record. We call the four record shares a profile. The initial change copied these four shares from the source calculation. It kept the recipient's total record weight, relative weights inside each record, weights outside the records, and original value vectors. We used correct-answer labels to choose and assess candidates, but the copying operation itself did not use those labels. The source profile came from a color question and was also used for other properties; we did not copy a value vector carrying the requested property's answer.

We ranked attention differences between correct and incorrect calculations across 36 layers with 32 heads each, or 1,152 heads, using the eight labeled search cases. We then tested the two leading candidates with supported positive differences. A fixed ranking rule compared each candidate with a control profile averaged from the other seven search worlds and selected layer 28, head 0; these indices start at zero. We tested that head and copying rule unchanged on all three recipient properties in the six remaining qualifying development worlds. This gave eight initially wrong and ten initially correct answers. Controls copied the unchanged calculation back into itself, used the average profile from the search cases, used a color profile from the same name, reversed the copying direction, or reassigned records in a cycle. Some controls deliberately predicted a particular wrong-object answer. Matching that prediction was scored separately from giving the correct factual answer.

Before running this later test, we required the repair to correct at least four of eight errors across at least three worlds, damage no more than one of ten correct answers, and correct at least two more errors than the fixed average-profile control. The reverse and cyclic controls each had to produce at least nine of 18 specified answers across at least three worlds. The cyclic control also had to reach at least two predicted object labels. These requirements were set before observing the results. They were not met, so this candidate did not proceed to independent confirmation.
Testing why the repair failed

After the failure, we fixed a follow-up plan and examined the same six worlds again. We kept the same head, cases, and answer-generation rule and did not tune the strength of the changes. For each property, we saved the head's output, attention weights, and recipient value vectors. Within each case, the record value vectors were exactly identical across the six unchanged combinations of two names and three properties. This is expected because the records come before the differing question in the shared input. It checks the implementation; it does not show that the vectors encode an abstract concept of the object.

We tested nine conditions: no change; the original color-question profile; the source profile from a question about the same property; the source token weights inside records; both its record shares and its within-record weights at the recipient's record total; its full contribution from record positions; its contribution from outside the records; its complete head output; and a random change of the same numerical size as the complete-head change. The record contribution was the sum of record value vectors multiplied by their attention weights. We defined the remaining contribution by subtracting this from the actual head output, keeping the small, explicitly bounded difference caused by numerical calculation. The complete-head source answered the same property correctly, so copying its output could also carry answer information. This was a comparison condition, not evidence of an answer-independent object-selection signal or a guarantee that no smaller change could work better.

We calculated each change once at the first answer step. At every later generation step, we recomputed the full sequence and applied that same change at the original question position. We did not move it to the newest token or adapt it to the generated answer. Each condition covered 18 recipient property questions, giving 162 complete answers. A new repair had to correct at least four errors across at least three worlds while damaging at most one initially correct answer. The complete-head change also had to correct at least two more errors than the matched random change. Only the random change and the complete-head change were matched in numerical size, measured by their vector norm. This control does not separate the effects of direction and size for the other changes.
Prediction scores and statistical analysis

The generator's balancing requirements determined the number of development worlds; we did not choose it through a statistical power calculation. We kept all answer-test responses, including badly formatted, unfinished, and inaccurate ones, and removed no outliers. The internal tests used cases selected by the stated correct-source and wrong-object rules. We knew the development answers and earlier test results when planning later stages. An unsupported numerical input would have stopped that planned test rather than been replaced by an easier case; none occurred in the reported repair test or follow-up.

We report counts, totals, and differences between worlds. For factual accuracy, we used a 95% descriptive range calculated by bootstrap resampling: we drew whole worlds with replacement 2,000 times, kept all repeated questions within each drawn world, and took the relevant percentiles. This procedure was fixed before the analysis and used random seed 20261114. These ranges describe variation in this artificial task; they do not guarantee performance across language models generally. We did not count repeated questions as independent trials, calculate binomial intervals for individual questions, or use the six-world follow-up to claim that a repair never works. The main claims did not use statistical significance tests.

We also examined saved scores without running the models again. At each answer step, a model assigns an unnormalized score, called a logit, to every possible next token. For each initial error, we subtracted the score of the first token of its original wrong answer from the score of one fixed, standard first token of the correct answer. We call this difference the score gap. We kept the original wrong token fixed after making changes. We also calculated the standard correct token's probability using scores over the full vocabulary and checked exact changes in the full score list. This measure differs from both complete-answer accuracy and the earlier search score, which combined acceptable spellings of answers. A better score gap did not count as a repair or lower the required success criteria. We kept results for each question and world.

After the original analysis, we added descriptive ranges for wrong-object answers and the main paired disagreements in S1 Data. They use 2,000 shared resamples of whole worlds with seed 20261115. We distinguish these later ranges from the original factual-accuracy ranges; they did not guide component selection or the success criteria.

Other exploratory checks asked whether answers followed the queried word or its position in the naming rules. We also fitted simple mixtures of rules that might predict which object's fact would be returned. Four fixed splits each used 24 worlds to fit the rules and eight different worlds to test them. Expanded comparisons added preferences for permanent object labels and middle record positions to the original eight cues. One analysis excluded the correct object before predicting which wrong object would be chosen. Because it used the correct-answer label to do this, it could not predict in advance whether the model would make a mistake. S1 Appendix describes the comparisons and their limits.
Data and code availability

S1 Data contains the prompts, recorded answers, values used in the figures, and records showing where the data came from. The public repository supplies code, processed results, and selected saved internal measurements. It does not yet include the complete original prediction-score files, so some numerical checks cannot be repeated from this release. The release metadata gives the current repository address, version, licenses, and exact data coverage.
Reproducibility and use of artificial intelligence tools

We saved the model's original scores for every possible next token at every generation step. Separate checks on an ordinary processor reconstructed the chosen tokens and decoded answers, checked that unchanged calculations reproduced their earlier sequences, and verified question positions, component calculations, file checksums, and counts of model evaluations. These checks used saved numbers; they did not rerun the models on that processor. An independently written grader read the printed object lists to determine the right answers instead of reusing the original scoring routine. All reported checks agreed. We fixed internal plans and source files before their respective execution stages, but did not publicly preregister the study or submit a Registered Report. The follow-up and later score analyses were planned after earlier development results were known.

OpenAI Codex assisted with planning, programming, running the experiments, analysis, literature checks, figure code, and drafting. We checked outputs with repeatable tests, source and data checksums, replay of complete saved outputs, and separately written answer checks. These automated checks do not replace the human author's scientific judgment. [The author must confirm the exact tools and model versions and describe their own review and approval before submission.] No artificial intelligence system is listed as an author. The study used imaginary object lists and publicly released model weights; it involved no human participants, animals, or personal participant data.
Results
Both models returned facts about the wrong object

Qwen answered 1,657 of 2,304 property questions correctly, or 71.92%. Its 95% range from resampling whole worlds was 64.71% to 78.47%. All 647 errors were finished answers giving another listed object's value for the requested property. Phi answered 1,980 of 2,304 correctly, or 85.94%, with a corresponding range of 82.77% to 88.93%. It gave another object's value 260 times and made 64 other property-answer errors. Wrong-object answers occurred in 30 of 32 worlds for Qwen and 26 of 32 for Phi. Table 1 summarizes the outcomes.

Permanent-label answers illustrate why formatting matters. Qwen gave the correct label alone in 384/512 cases. Phi met that strict requirement in only 21/512 cases. However, an additional check made after inspecting the results found 490 answers written as Object followed by a valid label; 476 named the correct object. Including the 21 correct labels given alone, 497/512 Phi answers identified the correct object under that secondary formatting check. We did not change the original strict score. Phi's low strict result therefore must not be described as evidence that it did not know which object was requested.
Names and list positions did not give one simple error rule

We asked whether answers stayed with a particular word when the two names exchanged positions, or instead stayed with the same line in the naming rules. There was no single pattern. Without highlighting, Qwen gave the same normalized answer across the four name-and-order combinations in 70/96 world-by-property comparisons: 61 always correct and nine always wrong. Four comparisons followed the name, seven followed the line position, and 15 fit neither exact pattern. Phi had 81/96 comparisons with the same answer throughout, two following the name, four following the line, and nine mixed. Some Phi differences were only formatting changes. These patterns describe the answers; they do not prove which internal process produced them.

Adding preferences for permanent object labels and list positions improved the combined rules' prediction of responses in worlds not used to fit them. Predictive loss, where a lower number indicates a better fit, fell from 0.860 to 0.816 per property answer for Qwen and from 0.543 to 0.532 for Phi. Even on questions the models got wrong, however, these combined rules still assigned the correct object the highest predicted probability. They did not fully explain when errors occurred. The released data include fuller comparisons allowing rules to vary by property and allowing preferences for particular answer words. These limited comparisons and name-order patterns do not rule out the retrieval processes described in earlier work [2].
The initial repair did not work reliably on other cases

Changing calculations before the requested property appeared had weak effects. In the tested heads, the first answer token changed in only one initial world where the answer scores were close to the choice boundary. This failure does not show that object information was missing at that stage; it only shows that the changes tested there did not provide the intended repair.

At the start of the answer, copying the correct-name color profile at the selected head made the first predicted token correct in five of eight search cases. This initial check concerned the first token, not the correctness of a complete generated answer. The mean improvement in the search score combining accepted answer spellings was 5.555, with an advantage of 2.041 over the average profile from the other seven search worlds. We then fixed the head and copying rule. In the six qualifying development worlds not used to choose the change, it corrected only one of eight complete wrong answers, in one world, while keeping all ten initially correct answers correct. The fixed average profile corrected none. The reverse and cyclic controls each produced their specified wrong-object answer in only 1/18 questions. blocks.text: Weights within the correct record stayed on the requested detail

Within the correct object's record, the share of attention on the tokens spelling the requested value averaged 94.98% for the eight search errors and 96.12% for the eight later test errors. Little went to tokens spelling other properties. The recipient's total weight on all object records was also high: approximately 94.9% in the search cases and 95.8% in the later cases. These measures did not show attention shifting away from the requested detail. They do not tell us what information the value vectors carried, so they cannot rule out the model computing with the wrong property information.
Further internal changes moved scores without adding correct answers

All 162 follow-up answers finished within two tokens, including the final end marker. Six new changes each corrected 0/8 errors: same-property record shares, within-record weights, both together, the full record contribution, the contribution from outside records, and the complete head output. Repeating the original color-profile change reproduced its earlier 1/8 repair exactly. Every condition kept all ten initially correct answers correct. The random control repaired none. Table 3 reports all nine conditions, rather than selecting only favorable results.

blocks.note: Each row covers 18 property questions in the same six development worlds. The last column averages the change in the score gap between one fixed standard correct first token and the fixed first token of the original wrong answer, across the eight initial errors. It is not complete-answer accuracy or the earlier score combining accepted spellings. The random change matches only the size of the whole-head change. Every condition other than no change altered all 18 saved first-step score lists; only the original color profile changed an answer.

blocks.text: The failed repairs were not simply changes that did nothing. Copying the complete source head changed the saved prediction scores on all 18 questions. On the eight initial errors, it improved the correct-versus-original-wrong score gap by 4.214 on average. The original mean gap was -10.904, so the mean remained negative. Copying the full record contribution gave a similar improvement of 4.207; copying the contribution from outside records gave only 0.003. None of the new conditions changed which first token the model chose. Fig 2 shows score changes for each error alongside the number of complete answers repaired. Changing the model's scores in favor of the correct token is therefore different from making it produce the correct answer.

Fig 2. Prediction scores changed without reliable answer repair. Panel A shows the change in the score gap between the fixed standard correct first token and the fixed first token of the original wrong answer. It covers eight initial errors in six worlds. Colors identify worlds; a black marker gives the mean. Two errors from the same world are related observations, not independent samples. Panel B shows complete answers repaired out of the same eight errors. All conditions kept ten initially correct answers correct. Copying the whole head and adding a random change are comparison tests, not bounds on possible repair success. Only the random change is matched in size to the whole-head change. These are reused development cases, not independent confirmation. Plotting code was developed with OpenAI Codex assistance using saved numerical outcomes.

All numerical replay checks and the separately written answer grader agreed. The 36 unchanged model evaluations exactly reproduced the original score lists. All 18 no-change answers and all 18 repetitions of the original color-profile change reproduced their earlier full sequences of saved scores. The calculation at the original query head showed zero drift. Recalculating saved component changes on an ordinary processor gave matching results, and checks covered all 360 saved model-evaluation outputs without running the models again. These checks support the negative result for the selected component, cases, and changes. They do not make it a result about every possible repair.
Discussion

Both models sometimes gave different facts for two names that the input explicitly assigned to the same object. These were not only formatting mistakes: many finished answers gave the requested property of a different listed object. The task separates giving a plausible value from giving the value of the object actually asked about. It does not establish that the models have no internal representation of objects, or that every error comes from a preference for a familiar meaning of a name.

The internal tests ask a narrower question: could copying one promising pattern from a correct calculation make a wrong calculation answer correctly? The selected head's weights contained useful information, and changing them affected the prediction scores. Yet the original copying rule repaired only one error in the six-world test, and no new version repaired an additional error. Copying more of the source calculation did not guarantee a better result. Replacing the whole head repaired none, whereas copying only its color-question record shares repaired one. Parts of a calculation can reinforce or cancel one another, so the whole-head result is not an upper bound on what a smaller change could achieve.

This illustrates the difference between affecting an answer and sufficiently explaining it [8,9]. One component can supply useful information while other parts of the model still favor the wrong answer. The positive score-gap changes cannot be explained by adding the same number to every candidate score: the correct token improved relative to the original wrong token. But this does not identify a general answer-word boosting process or show that the head contains a reusable control for choosing an object. The cause could involve several cooperating components, later calculations that use the information differently in different contexts, or a more widely distributed process. Our tests do not distinguish these remaining possibilities.

The results add to earlier work rather than overturn it. Previous studies already showed that correctly identifying a named item can coexist with using the wrong property [1], that word-based and position-based retrieval can coexist [2], and that models can update or organize object-to-property links internally [3,4]. Our added evidence is the full test sequence in a controlled fictional setting: a promising change was fixed, failed on other cases, and remained unreliable when we tested its parts. This does not disprove the processes found in those studies or mean that attention is always uninformative [6,7].
Limitations

We tested two small models trained to follow instructions, eight additional-name words, two wording formats, and one kind of artificial task. Words recurred across worlds. We balanced specified positions and roles, not every possible combination. The numerical settings may differ from the lower-precision settings often used to run these models. The answer pattern appeared in two model families, but the internal repair was tested only in Qwen. Formatting also limits any claim that identifying an object and retrieving its properties are completely separate abilities, especially for Phi.

The internal tests deliberately selected cases with a reliable correct source and a finished wrong-object answer to change. Eight errors across six worlds do not estimate how often a repair would work on all model errors. We designed the follow-up after seeing the initial failure and reused the same worlds; the reserved confirmation worlds were not evaluated. We did not search every component or establish that the same failure applies across model families. Keeping answers correct refers only to the ten tested property answers. Not changing other queries is not evidence that unrelated facts or tasks would also be preserved.

Copying from a source question about the same property can carry answer information, rather than only information about which object to choose. Also, the random control matches the size of only the whole-head change, not every change. The comparisons cannot establish what each direction in the calculation means. Our score gap considers one standard first token for each answer and omits other accepted spellings; it cannot replace scoring complete answers. Fixing plans and code before execution helps others trace the work, but is not public preregistration. The study's contribution is this particular controlled example and test sequence, not a claim to have discovered a fundamentally new mechanism.
Implications for further work

A stronger claim about how models choose an object would need a change selected before seeing the results of an independent test. That test should use new contexts with reassigned property values. Copying an object-selection pattern should then return the recipient object's own facts, even when they differ from the source's facts. It should also produce the specified effects when reversed, preserve other relevant answers, and work in another model family. These are next-study requirements, not achievements of this study. The present results give a reason not to treat this one head as a proven reusable fix.
Conclusions

Two names for the same object sometimes produced different factual answers in both models on the same 32 balanced development worlds. A proposed internal change in Qwen looked promising at first, but did not reliably repair complete answers on other development cases. Nine follow-up conditions added no new repair, even though the changes affected prediction scores and often favored the correct answer's first token. The naming failure is reproducible in this setting; the tested repair is insufficient. Why the models make these errors remains unresolved.
